metadata.title: Beyond the test scores: Balancing information and accountability in global assessment systems

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata with a nested sampling design (students within schools within economies) and applies PISA final student weights at Level 1 and final school weights at Level 2, as stated in the Data analyses section. Descriptive statistics for student-level variables are computed using PISA final student weights, and standard errors are estimated using balanced repeated replication (BRR) with 80 replicate weights following OECD technical guidelines. For economy-level variables (N=65), descriptive statistics are unweighted with each economy weighted as unity, consistent with the economy-level aggregation approach. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly indicates complex-survey weight usage and BRR-based uncertainty estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that it excluded economies lacking valid information on test frequency or accountability, but it does not describe any student-level missing-data handling procedure for the analytic sample (e.g., imputation vs. complete-case rules). Because PISA uses plausible values for mathematics and the authors combine results across the ten PVs using Rubin’s rules, missingness handling is still required for transparency about how incomplete questionnaire/test participation was treated. This omission is a reporting gap: the methodology does not specify whether missing covariates were imputed or whether cases with missing background variables were removed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 mathematics achievement for 15-year-old students across 81 participating economies, then excluded economies lacking valid information on test frequency or test-based accountability. The final analytic sample includes 65 economies, 17,783 schools, and 479,178 students. The dependent variable uses all ten mathematics plausible values, and the analysis is restricted to the specified multilevel structure (students nested within schools nested within economies). No additional student-level inclusion/exclusion rules for missing background variables are explicitly described.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level HLM (Stata mixed; ML estimation with PVs combined via Rubin’s rules). Key coefficients (standardized): accountability β=-0.128 (p<.05) in M2; frequency β=0.149 (p<.05) in M2; interaction accountability×frequency β=0.021 (ns) in M3. Control effects in M1: gender β=0.088 (p<.001), ESCS β=0.111 (p<.001), immigration β=-0.046 (p<.001), school ESCS β=0.329 (p<.001), GDP β=0.426 (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics the study leveraged test-based accountability (STDTEST), test frequency, and socioeconomic controls (ESCS, school ESCS) plus national GDP to model mathematics achievement, finding that stronger accountability was negatively associated with achievement (β≈-0.13) while higher test frequency was positively associated (β≈0.15), with no significant accountability×frequency interaction. This indicates that calibrating assessment systems toward frequent, low-stakes informational use and away from coercive high-stakes accountability may improve achievement and reduce equity risks, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics (15-year-olds), cross-level moderation by SES and GDP
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cross-level interactions (standardized coefficients, Table 4): accountability×student ESCS β=-0.029 (p<.001) and accountability×school ESCS β=-0.052 (p<.001), indicating stronger adverse accountability effects in more advantaged contexts. Frequency×student ESCS β=-0.026 (p<.001) and frequency×school ESCS β=-0.033 (p<.001), indicating larger frequency benefits for lower-SES students/schools. Accountability×GDP β=-0.078 (ns) and frequency×GDP β=-0.009 (ns), indicating no systematic moderation by GDP.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics the study leveraged test-based accountability and test frequency together with SES moderators (student ESCS and school ESCS) to predict mathematics achievement, finding that accountability’s negative association is stronger in higher-SES students and schools (accountability×ESCS and accountability×school ESCS negative and significant) while test frequency shows larger positive associations for lower-SES students and schools (frequency×ESCS and frequency×school ESCS negative and significant). This indicates that assessment policy design should be equity-sensitive—supporting disadvantaged learners through frequent informational testing while limiting coercive accountability pressure in advantaged contexts—though the results remain correlational due to cross-sectional PISA data.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 mathematics data for 15-year-old students from 65 economies (479,178 students; 17,783 schools) and models mathematics achievement using a three-level hierarchical linear model with ten mathematics plausible values combined via Rubin’s rules. It estimates how two economy-level policy instruments—test frequency (principal-reported) and test-based accountability (STDTEST)—relate to achievement, net of student (gender, ESCS, immigration), school (school ESCS, student–teacher ratio, school type), and economy (log GDP) controls. In the main specification, test-based accountability shows a negative association with achievement (β≈-0.13, p<.01) while test frequency shows a positive association (β≈0.15, p<.01), and the accountability×frequency interaction is not significant. Cross-level moderation indicates accountability is more harmful in higher-SES contexts and frequency is more beneficial for lower-SES contexts, with no significant moderation by GDP. Limitations include cross-sectional inference and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling at the student level.
